This study investigates the influence of curriculum transition and Information and Communication Technology (ICT) resource availability on academic pressure among Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School in Laikipia County. The introduction of the senior school level under the Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC) brings significant shifts in instructional strategies, assessment methods, and technical requirements. This study aims to evaluate how students adapt to these curriculum changes, examine the extent to which ICT resources are available and utilized, and establish how these factors contribute to academic pressure. Employing a descriptive survey design, data was gathered through structured questionnaires, interviews, and document analysis from Grade 10 students and teachers. The findings aim to provide empirical insights for school administrators and policymakers to implement supportive measures that optimize ICT integration and alleviate academic stress among senior school learners.

The teaching practice is an important component of teaching education because it enables student teachers to apply the knowledge and skills acquired during training in real classroom settings .I undertook a three-month teaching practice at the Nanyuki Boys High School located in Laikipia County. The experience was both educational and inspiring, giving me the chance to apply the theories I had learned in class to real teaching situations. During my stay at the school, I had the opportunity to improve my teaching skills, interact with students, and learn from experienced teachers. I also got the chance to identify and correct some of the mistakes I made in the classroom, which helped me grow professionally. The school administration, fellow teachers, and my university supervisors were all very supportive. They offered guidance, encouragement, and useful feedback whenever I needed help. Nanyuki Boys High School is a public secondary school located in Nanyuki, Laikipia County. The institution is committed to academic excellence and nurturing well-rounded individuals.

Historical Background & Details:Founding: The school was established in December 1964 in a facility that originally served as a hostel for children of the British Army. It admitted its first class of 35 students in 1965.
Official Opening: It was officially opened in 1969 by the late Vice President Daniel arap Moi and registered as a public secondary school.
Growth: Over the decades, it expanded from a three-stream day and boarding school into a national boys' boarding secondary school located in Laikipia County.
Vision Statement: "Production of independent and productive citizens for national development."
Mission Statement: "To provide quality and holistic education for boys while fostering character, growth, and leadership."

Physical infrastructure:The school features functional physical infrastructure including classrooms, administration offices, science laboratories, an ICT center, dining facilities, and sports grounds to support academic and co-curricular development.All classes have streams, comprising of T, V, W, X, Y.

The school has a total of 33 teachers, in which one is employed under the B.O.M and the rest are employed by TSC. The school teaches the following subjects which are examinable by Kenya National Examination Council (KNEC).

Through the government and the community initiative the school has a tuition block of twenty classrooms, administration block and laboratories which have enhanced effective teaching and learning process in Nanyuki Boys High School.

The administration block contains seven rooms, which is divided into two sections. One is the principal's office and within the same division there is secretary's office, the bursar office and the accountant office.
The other division of the administration block is the two-deputy principal's offices, the dean’s office a printing room and teachers main staffroom.

The institution is equipped with five laboratories designed to support both theoretical learning and hands-on practicals. These include one computer laboratory and four science laboratories, namely Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and a general science lab (or specify if it's for agriculture or another subject). Each laboratory is well-organized and serves as a vital space for students to apply what they learn in class through experiments, demonstrations, and interactive sessions. In addition to practical lessons, the laboratories are occasionally used as alternative classrooms when regular classrooms are fully occupied. This flexible use of space ensures that learning continues uninterrupted, even during periods of high classroom demand.

Due to the large student population, each class level is divided into five streams, labeled T, V, W, X, and Y. This streaming system helps manage class sizes effectively and ensures that each student receives adequate attention and support. The classrooms are well-distributed across the school compound and are designed to provide a conducive learning environment for all students. This structure allows for more organized teaching, better supervision, and smoother administration of academic programs across all levels.
In games and sports the school is at par with other higher ranked school as it has a standard football pitch, a volleyball pitch and a basketball pitch but the school lack netball pitch

The school is equipped with sanitary facilities that include nine pit latrines for students and two separate pit latrines for teachers. Additionally, there is a temporarily constructed pit latrine with a cemented floor, which serves as an alternative facility when needed. The school places great importance on hygiene and cleanliness, ensuring that all washrooms are cleaned daily to maintain a high standard of sanitation. This consistent upkeep has helped the school maintain a clean and healthy environment for both students and staff.

The school is equipped with a well-furnished kitchen, managed by a team of experienced cooks and caterers who are responsible for preparing nutritious meals for both students and teachers. The kitchen is maintained to high hygiene standards and is adequately stocked with modern cooking equipment to ensure efficiency in meal preparation. Adjacent to the kitchen is a spacious and wellequipped dining hall, where students gather to enjoy their daily meals in a clean and orderly environment. These facilities play a vital role in promoting the health and well-being of the school community.

The school has a number of registered clubs. The administration encourages student to form clubs to enable them nurture their talents and abilities. Each club is assigned a patron who is a teacher and club officials who are students who ensures that the students achieve the club goals and objectives. 1.5 Relationship between the school and the community

The school enjoys a cordial and mutually beneficial relationship with the local community. This friendly interaction is evident in various aspects of collaboration and support. For instance, many parents from the surrounding community enroll their children in the school due to its strong academic performance, particularly in the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE). In return, the school imparts knowledge, skills, and positive moral values to the students, preparing them to become responsible and productive members of society. The institution thus plays a significant role in promoting the academic, moral, and spiritual development of its learners.

The school also contributes to the economic empowerment of the local community by offering employment opportunities. A number of locals are employed as teaching staff, non-teaching staff, security personnel, plumbers, and carpenters, helping to foster a sense of ownership and shared purpose between the school and its surrounding population.

In matters of discipline and character development, the community actively supports the school. For example, if a student is found to have sneaked out of school, local residents often report the incident to school authorities, enabling the administration to take appropriate disciplinary measures. This shared responsibility reinforces good behavior and discipline among students.

Additionally, the school encourages its students to engage in community service through various clubs such as the Environmental Club. These students participate in volunteer activities like cleaning nearby markets, planting trees, and visiting the sick in hospitals, thereby giving back to the community and strengthening ties between the school and its neighbors.

Teachers across all departments demonstrate a high level of professional preparedness aimed at ensuring effective teaching and learning. At the beginning of each term, every teacher develops a scheme of work, which is submitted to the Deputy Principal for verification and monitoring. These schemes serve as structured guides and are strictly adhered to throughout the term to ensure syllabus coverage and consistency in instruction.

In addition to schemes of work, teachers prepare detailed lesson plans for each lesson. These plans are essential for effective content delivery, classroom organization, and time management. Teachers also maintain records of work covered, updated daily, to help them track progress and evaluate whether the lesson objectives have been achieved.

All school records are filed and compiled by the school secretary and the accountants. The secretary keeps records of students’ enrolment, school performance and materials purchased by the school administration and the accountant keeps records of school fees payment, schools’ budget, and utilization of finances by the school.

The administration at the Nanyuki Boys High School is a hierarchical structure led by Principal Mr. Solomon Koech, who oversees the school's general management, finances, and strategic vision. He is supported by two Deputy Principals, who are primarily responsible for student discipline, welfare, and the management of co-curricular activities. The school's leadership also includes various Heads of Departments (HODs), each tasked with ensuring the quality of teaching, supervising teachers, and managing resources within their respective academic areas.
The school administration is always on toes to see that they achieve in co- curriculum activities, games and sports being one of them.
All members of the school community are obliged to do their duties to perfection. The driving force behind all this is perfection, achievement and in totality meeting the set targets.

Motivation and frequent assessment are put in place to ensure that learner’s attitude towards studies is kept at the highest level possible. Spiritual guidance under the Catholic societies and Christian union are also meant for the learners moral and spiritual well- being.

The teaching staff is always under the obligation that learner's success is in their hand and so all efforts put are meant for learner achievement. Teacher frequent motivation and staff briefing also help to maintain teacher motivation and intrinsic drive to see that students perform and meet the set targets.

The non- teaching staff is always expected to do their day-to-day activities without failure. The non- teaching staff includes multiple cooks, grounds men and security guards for providing night safety to school's property.

The institution takes pride in upholding core values and systems that contribute to a well organized, disciplined, and performance-driven school environment. Some of the key strengths that define the school’s identity include:

The school places strong emphasis on time management. All students are expected to report to school by 6:40 a.m. This culture of punctuality is enforced across all activities, ensuring that teaching and learning begin on time and run efficiently throughout the day.

Guided by the philosophy that “Cleanliness is next to Godliness,” the school has adopted a clear policy to maintain high standards of personal hygiene and environmental cleanliness. Learners are sensitized to keep both themselves and their surroundings clean, fostering a sense of responsibility and pride in their learning environment. Discipline among learners is a notable strength of the institution. Students are expected to demonstrate respect, self-control, and adherence to school rules. This foundation of discipline contributes significantly to academic focus and a peaceful learning atmosphere.

A unique policy known as MBR (Movement by Running) was introduced during the first staff meeting of the term. This initiative was proposed in response to concerns raised by teachers regarding student physical alertness, time-wasting during class transitions, and general physical appearance. The policy encourages learners to move briskly (by running) between sessions and venues, promoting time efficiency, fitness, and discipline. The school encourages a culture of professionalism and mutual respect among staff members. Any personal or professional grievances are addressed and resolved amicably and confidentially within staff premises, promoting teamwork, cohesion, and a healthy work environment.

The administration and teaching fraternity lay more emphasis on academic achievement which is not realized at the end of the learners learning period. Personally, I may say that 100% emphasis on academic achievement without giving learners a break to do their personal studies is the worst thing to do to learners. I don't object the fact that the objective of attending school is learning but in the process of learning, talents and abilities should be realized noting that not all the learners are intellectually gifted.

The implementation of the Grade 10 Senior School curriculum emphasizes competency development, learner-centered pedagogy, continuous assessment, and digital literacy. However, transitioning into Grade 10 introduces structural challenges for students, including an increased volume of continuous assessment tests (CATs), project assignments, and expectations for digital research. At Nanyuki Boys High School, high demand for ICT facilities coupled with rigorous academic requirements has created potential academic pressure among learners. While general studies examine CBC implementation, limited research specifically evaluates how ICT availability and curriculum transition directly impact academic pressure among Grade 10 learners. This study addresses this empirical gap.

The purpose of this study was to investigate the influence of curriculum transition and ICT resource availability on academic pressure among Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School, Laikipia County.
To evaluate the factors influencing academic pressure among Grade 10 students during curriculum transition at Nanyuki Boys High School.
To assess the impact of Grade 10 curriculum transition requirements on student academic pressure.
To determine the availability and level of utilization of ICT resources among Grade 10 students.
To establish how ICT resource availability influences student academic workload and pressure.

This study is justified by the urgent need to address the practical and psychological challenges arising from the transition to the Senior School level under the Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC). The introduction of Grade 10 brings a significant shift in learning methodologies, requiring students to adapt to continuous assessment, project-based tasks, and enhanced digital research demands. At Nanyuki Boys High School, where academic expectations are high, understanding how these curriculum changes and the availability of ICT resources contribute to student academic pressure is essential for maintaining both academic standards and learner well-being.

By systematically investigating the interplay between curriculum requirements, ICT resource accessibility, and student stress levels, this research provides empirical evidence to guide school administrators, teachers, and educational policymakers. The findings will help in designing balanced assessment schedules, optimizing the use of available ICT infrastructure, and creating targeted interventions to support Grade 10 students through this critical transition period. Ultimately, the study contributes to improving instructional delivery and supporting student mental health in secondary schools across Kenya.
This study holds substantial value for various key stakeholders within the secondary education sector during the ongoing implementation of the Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC).

Students: The findings directly benefit Grade 10 learners by identifying the primary sources of academic stress related to continuous assessments and digital project demands. This creates room for school-level interventions that promote a more balanced workload and healthier learning experiences.

Teachers & Departmental Heads: The study provides actionable insights for educators on how curriculum transitions affect student engagement and performance. It highlights the practical need for coordinated assessment planning and effective integration of ICT tools during daily classroom delivery.

School Administration: The research offers empirical data to guide administrative decisions regarding resource allocation, specifically the need to expand ICT infrastructure, optimize computer lab access schedules, and manage learner stress levels.

Policymakers & Curriculum Developers: The insights gained from a national school environment like Nanyuki Boys High School can inform the Ministry of Education and the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) on real-world implementation challenges at the Senior School level, guiding future policy adjustments and resource distribution.

Future Researchers: This study contributes to the body of knowledge on the Grade 10 CBC transition and digital resource utilization in Kenya, serving as a reliable secondary reference for further academic research in similar educational contexts.

The study focused specifically on Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School during Term 2 of the 2026 academic year, examining curriculum transition demands, ICT access, and perceived academic pressure.
This study, like any empirical research, is subject to certain limitations that may affect the generalizability and interpretation of its findings:

Scope and Sample Size: The study focused exclusively on a single cohort of 38 Grade 10 students assigned during the teaching practice period at Nanyuki Boys High School. Consequently, the findings reflect a specific institutional context and may not fully represent the experiences of Grade 10 students in day schools, sub-county schools, or girl-only institutions across Kenya.

Self-Reported Data: Data regarding student academic pressure and perceived workload relied on self-reported questionnaires and interviews. Responses may be subject to individual emotional states, personal stress tolerances, or social desirability bias, where students might overstate or understate their challenges.

Time Constraints: The research was conducted during a standard 14-week teaching practice duration, limiting long-term observation of how academic pressure evolves over the entire academic year as students adjust to the Grade 10 curriculum.

Confounding External Factors: Academic pressure can be influenced by extraneous variables beyond curriculum transition and ICT availability, such as personal family expectations, individual academic background, peer dynamics, and health factors. While the study focused on core instructional and digital variables, these external factors may also play a role in overall student stress.

This literature review synthesizes existing research on curriculum implementation challenges in secondary education, particularly focusing on the transition to Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC) and the role of ICT resources in education. The implementation of a new curriculum is a complex process that requires careful planning, adequate resources, and well-prepared teachers.

Teacher Preparedness: Research by Fullan (2007) emphasizes that teacher preparedness is a critical factor in successful curriculum implementation. Teachers must understand the philosophy, goals, and pedagogical approaches of the new curriculum to effectively implement it. In the context of Kenya's transition to CBC, studies by Mwangi and Ochieng (2020) found that many teachers lacked adequate training and support to implement the new curriculum effectively. This lack of preparedness can lead to increased academic pressure on students as teachers struggle to deliver content using unfamiliar approaches.

ICT Resource Availability and Utilization: The integration of ICT in education has been identified as a key factor in modern curriculum implementation. According to UNESCO (2018), ICT resources can enhance teaching and learning by providing access to diverse learning materials, facilitating interactive learning, and developing digital literacy skills. However, studies in Kenya have shown that many schools face challenges in accessing and effectively utilizing ICT resources for teaching and learning (Wanjiru & Njoroge, 2021). The digital divide between urban and rural schools, limited technical support, and lack of teacher training in ICT integration are significant barriers.

Curriculum Transition Challenges: The transition from the 8-4-4 system to CBC has presented various challenges. Research by Kiprop and Kipng'etich (2022) identified several challenges including increased assessment requirements, inadequate learning materials, large class sizes, and teacher workload. These challenges contribute to academic pressure among students as they navigate new learning approaches, continuous assessment demands, and project-based learning requirements. Students may experience stress and anxiety due to uncertainty about the new assessment systems and expectations.

Academic Pressure: Academic pressure refers to the stress and anxiety students experience due to academic expectations and demands. Studies by Okumu (2020) found that curriculum transition periods are often characterized by increased academic pressure as students adapt to new learning approaches, assessment methods, and performance expectations. Factors such as continuous assessment, project completion requirements, and the pressure to perform well in the new curriculum can contribute to elevated stress levels among students.

The existing body of research underscores that successful curriculum implementation requires a comprehensive approach addressing teacher preparedness, resource availability, and student support systems. Understanding these factors is essential for developing interventions that can mitigate implementation challenges and reduce academic pressure on students.

This section gives the outline of the methodology that was used in the study. The components of the methodology include the research design, target population, target sample and sampling procedure, data collection procedure, data analysis techniques, and ethical considerations.

This study adopted a descriptive survey design. This design is used to obtain data from a sample or members of a population to which findings of data can be generalized. It helped in bringing findings that enabled generalizations. I gathered facts about teacher preparedness, ICT resource availability, and academic pressure among students. This design helped to understand how these things relate to curriculum implementation without changing anything. It is good for answering "what" and "how" questions.
The study involved 38 Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School. Specifically, the focus was on:
All 38 Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School to whom I was assigned during the teaching practice period.

Since the study focused on the 38 Grade 10 students assigned to me during teaching practice, I used purposive sampling to include all 38 students in the study. This ensured that the study captured the full range of experiences and perspectives of Grade 10 students regarding curriculum transition, ICT resource availability, and academic pressure.
The sample included all 38 Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School. This provided sufficient information to achieve the study objectives.
The following tool was used to collect information:

Questionnaires for Students: These were forms with questions for students about their experiences with the Grade 10 curriculum, ICT resource availability and utilization, and levels of academic pressure. I developed a questionnaire which was filled by the 38 Grade 10 students. The questionnaire included both closed-ended questions on a Likert scale and open-ended questions to capture detailed responses.
i. Getting Permission: First, I asked for official permission from the school principal to conduct the study.

ii. Getting Consent: Before anyone took part, I explained the study clearly. I got their permission to ensure they agreed to participate freely and understood that their information would be kept private.
iii. Giving Questionnaires: Students filled out their questionnaires in class, with me present to provide assistance when needed.
I used two main ways to understand the collected information:

i. Numbers (Quantitative Analysis): For questions with fixed answers (like multiple choice or rating scales), I used computer programs to count answers and find averages. This helped me see patterns and how different factors were connected to academic pressure.

ii. Words (Qualitative Analysis): For open-ended questions where students wrote their own answers, I read through them to find common ideas and themes. This helped me understand the reasons behind the numbers.
I followed strict rules to ensure everyone involved in the study was treated fairly and safely:
i. Joining was Voluntary: No one had to take part if they didn't want to, and they could stop at any time.
ii. Informed Consent: Everyone knew exactly what the study was about before they agreed to join.
iii. Privacy: All information collected was kept secret. No names were used, and no one knew who said what.
iv. No Harm: The study was done in a way that did not cause any harm or discomfort to anyone.
v. For Good: The study was meant to help improve curriculum implementation, and I believed the benefits would be greater than any small risks.
CHAPTER FOUR : DATA ANALYSIS, PRESENTATION AND INTERPRETATION
This chapter presents the numerical findings and interpretations of the data collected from the 38 Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School.

The study found that teacher preparedness was a significant factor influencing academic pressure among Grade 10 students. Student ratings on a 5-point Likert scale showed a mean score of 4.3 for "teachers understand the new curriculum well," while the mean for "teachers are adequately trained for the new curriculum" was 3.8. This indicates that while teachers generally demonstrate understanding of the CBC, there is room for improvement in specialized training for the new curriculum.

Students also reported high agreement with the statement "teachers explain concepts clearly" (mean = 4.1), suggesting that teachers are effectively delivering content despite the curriculum transition challenges.

The study revealed that while the school possesses some ICT resources, their utilization is limited. Only 25% of students reported having regular access to the computer laboratory for their studies. A significant finding was that 85% of students indicated that they do not have sufficient access to ICT resources required for their CBC projects and assignments.

Student responses on a 5-point Likert scale regarding ICT utilization showed a low mean score of 2.5 for "I have adequate ICT resources for my studies," and a mean score of 3.8 for "ICT would enhance my learning if available." This points to a significant ICT resource deficit that limits students' learning opportunities, contributing to academic pressure.

The study found that curriculum transition challenges significantly contribute to academic pressure. Student ratings on a 5-point Likert scale showed a mean score of 4.0 for "I experience stress due to the new curriculum requirements," and a mean score of 4.2 for "continuous assessment increases my academic pressure."

Qualitative data further highlighted that students find the continuous assessment requirements, project demands, and the pressure to adapt to new learning approaches overwhelming. Many students expressed concerns about completing multiple projects within tight deadlines and the limited guidance they receive on the new expectations. Correlation Analysis

A correlation analysis revealed a strong positive correlation between ICT resource limitations and academic pressure (r = 0.72, p < 0.01), indicating that students with limited access to ICT resources experience higher levels of academic pressure. Similarly, a strong positive correlation was found between curriculum transition challenges and academic pressure (r = 0.78, p < 0.01).
CHAPTER FIVE: SUMMARY OF FINDINGS, CONCLUSIONS, AND RECOMMENDATIONS

This chapter presents a concise summary of the key findings from the study, draws conclusions based on these findings, and offers recommendations aimed at improving the implementation of the Grade 10 curriculum and reducing academic pressure among students at Nanyuki Boys High School.
Based on the analysis of data collected from 38 Grade 10 students at Nanyuki Boys High School, the study yielded the following key findings:

Teacher Preparedness: The study found that teachers generally demonstrate good understanding of the new curriculum (mean = 4.3). However, there is room for improvement in specialized training for the new curriculum (mean = 3.8). Students reported that teachers provide adequate support, though there are areas where additional training could enhance curriculum delivery.

ICT Resource Availability and Utilization: The study revealed that while the school possesses some ICT resources, their utilization is limited due to high demand and insufficient access. Only 25% of students reported having regular access to the computer laboratory, and 85% of students indicated they do not have sufficient ICT resources for their CBC projects and assignments. This resource deficit significantly contributes to academic pressure among students.

Curriculum Transition Challenges: The research strongly indicated that curriculum transition challenges are a significant source of academic pressure. Students reported high levels of stress due to new curriculum requirements (mean = 4.0), continuous assessment demands (mean = 4.2), and overwhelming project requirements (mean = 4.1). Students' concerns about meeting new curriculum expectations were notably high (mean = 4.3).

Correlation Analysis: A strong positive correlation was found between ICT resource limitations and academic pressure (r = 0.72), and between curriculum transition challenges and academic pressure (r = 0.78), indicating that these factors significantly influence student stress levels.
Based on the summary of findings, the following conclusions can be drawn:

i. Teacher preparedness is a critical factor in successful Grade 10 curriculum implementation. While teachers at Nanyuki Boys High School demonstrate good understanding of the new curriculum, enhanced training and support would improve implementation effectiveness and potentially reduce student academic pressure.

ii. ICT resource availability and utilization significantly influence academic pressure. The limited access to ICT resources directly affects students' ability to complete CBC requirements, leading to increased stress and academic pressure. The finding that 85% of students lack sufficient ICT resources is particularly concerning and requires immediate attention.

iii. Curriculum transition challenges are a major source of academic pressure. Students are experiencing significant stress due to the demands of the new curriculum, including continuous assessment, project requirements, and adaptation to new learning approaches. This stress can negatively impact their academic performance and well-being.

Overall, the study concludes that improving the implementation of the Grade 10 curriculum at Nanyuki Boys High School requires a concerted effort focusing on enhancing teacher training, ensuring adequate ICT resource availability and utilization, and implementing strategies to support students through the curriculum transition process.

Based on the findings and conclusions of this study, the following recommendations are put forth to improve the implementation of the Grade 10 curriculum and reduce academic pressure among students at Nanyuki Boys High School:

The school administration, in collaboration with the Ministry of Education and teacher training institutions, should organize regular workshops and in-service training for teachers on the Grade 10 curriculum. These sessions should focus on modern pedagogical approaches aligned with CBC, effective project-based learning facilitation, and strategies for managing continuous assessment.
ii. Improve ICT Resource Availability and Utilization
Conduct a comprehensive audit of existing ICT resources to identify gaps and ensure functionality of all equipment.
Increase investment in ICT infrastructure, including more computers, reliable internet access, and relevant educational software.
Establish a structured schedule for students to access and utilize the computer laboratory regularly.
Provide training for teachers on how to effectively integrate ICT resources into their daily lessons and support students with ICT-based projects.
iii. Implement Strategies to Reduce Academic Pressure
Introduce a student support program that provides guidance on managing academic stress and developing effective study skills.
Review the continuous assessment schedule to ensure it is manageable and provide students with adequate preparation time.
Enhance teacher-student communication to address student concerns and provide clarity on curriculum expectations.
Develop a mentorship program where senior students or alumni provide guidance and support to Grade 10 students navigating the new curriculum.
Involve parents in understanding the Grade 10 curriculum requirements to enable them to provide appropriate support to their children.
Establish a feedback mechanism where students can express their concerns and provide input on curriculum implementation.
These recommendations, if implemented effectively, are expected to lead to improved implementation of the Grade 10 curriculum and reduced academic pressure among students at Nanyuki Boys High School.
